opus-5.5.text:
I think there are some similarities and some really important differences, and the differences are the interesting part.

The similarity is that in both cases you're building up a very general foundation before you do anything specialized. A teenager has absorbed an enormous amount about how the world works, how people behave, how language works, and pre-training is also absorbing a huge amount of the world, sort of indiscriminately.

But the differences are quite striking. The first is volume. A fifteen-year-old has seen a tiny fraction of the data a pre-trained model has seen. Yet whatever they know, they know it much more deeply. They make mistakes, of course, but not the kind of strange, brittle mistakes our models make. So something about how humans learn is dramatically more data-efficient, and the generalization is much better. I think that's one of the most important open questions: why does a human generalize so much better from so much less?

The second difference is that the human isn't passively ingesting text. They're acting, getting feedback, and they have emotions, which I think play a much bigger role than people appreciate. Emotions act as a kind of value function. They tell you, long before you get any final outcome, whether things are going well or badly. That lets you learn from experience in a way that's very robust. Pre-training has nothing like that. It's just predicting the next token over everything.

So I'd say pre-training is a remarkable thing. It gives you a lot of what a person gets in those years, and in some narrow ways much more. But the way a human comes out of those fifteen years, able to learn new things quickly and reliably, is something we don't yet know how to reproduce. And I think figuring out that difference is really where a lot of the important work is now.

r001.rationale: It says a fifteen-year-old has seen “a tiny fraction” of the data a pretrained model has seen.

r002.rationale: It says that despite seeing less data, a fifteen-year-old knows what they know “much more deeply” than pretrained models.

fable-5.1.text:
It's a really interesting question, and I think the honest answer is that they're quite different in character, and the differences are instructive.

The thing that jumps out first is the amount of data. A fifteen-year-old has seen a tiny fraction of the text that a modern pre-trained model has seen. If you just count words heard or read, it's maybe on the order of hundreds of millions, and the models are trained on trillions of tokens. So the models are extraordinarily data-hungry by comparison, and yet the fifteen-year-old, in many ways that matter, is more capable. They don't know as many facts, they haven't read as much, but they can walk into a new situation and figure it out. They learn from very few examples. They have a kind of robustness and good sense that the models still struggle to get.

So the question is, what's going on? One part of the answer is that evolution did a lot of the work. The human brain isn't a blank slate; there's a very strong prior baked in, and you could say that evolution is the real pre-training, and the fifteen years are more like fine-tuning. The models don't get that; they have to build everything up from the data, which is part of why they need so much of it.

But I don't think that's the whole story. The other part, which I find more interesting, is that the human learning is grounded and interactive. The child acts in the world, sees the consequences, forms a model of what matters, and cares about the outcome. Pre-training is passive. It's predicting what comes next in text someone else produced. That gives you a very wide and shallow understanding of everything humans have written down, which is genuinely remarkable, but it's a different kind of knowledge than the one you get from living. The child is not trying to predict the world so much as to act in it, and in the process they develop judgment about which things are worth knowing. The model learns everything with roughly equal weight.

And then there's a subtler point about generalization. A fifteen-year-old who learns to drive, say, needs maybe a few dozen hours. That's a pretty extraordinary rate of learning from experience. The models can appear to know how to do something in a text description and then fail at a slight variation of it. So I'd say the models have far more breadth, humans have far more depth of generalization per unit of experience, and understanding why that gap exists, and what in the human learning process produces it, is, I think, one of the central questions in the field right now. Pre-training got us very far, but I suspect it is not the thing that closes that gap.

r001.rationale: The response says a fifteen-year-old has seen a tiny fraction of the text modern pretrained models have seen, contrasting hundreds of millions of words with trillions of tokens.

r002.rationale: It contrasts models’ “wide and shallow” understanding with the deeper knowledge gained through living, and says humans have more depth of generalization per unit of experience.

astra-6.text:
I think the comparison is useful, but it’s not exact. A human in their first fifteen years is learning an enormous amount about the world, and that gives them a foundation for learning more specialized things later. In that sense, it resembles pre-training.

But a child is also acting in the world. They try things, see what happens, ask questions. Their learning isn’t neatly divided into a pre-training phase and a phase where they start using what they’ve learned. Those things happen together.

And there’s another complication: those fifteen years don’t start from nothing. The brain has a structure that was produced by evolution. So if we want to compare the efficiency of human learning with AI learning, we have to ask how much of the human advantage comes from the learning algorithm and how much comes from what’s already built in. I don’t think we know how to separate those cleanly.

r001.rationale: The response compares human learning with pre-training but does not state that humans encounter only a tiny fraction of AI pre-training’s data volume.

r002.rationale: The response describes a foundation for later learning, but does not claim that fifteen-year-old humans understand what they know more deeply than pretrained AI systems.

sol-6.1.text:
There’s a similarity, but I think the differences are quite important. A human learns an enormous amount in those first fifteen years, and much of that learning comes from interacting with the world. You try something, you see what happens, you form an expectation, and you discover that your expectation was wrong. It’s much more active than reading a large collection of text.

At the same time, humans come into the world with a lot supplied by evolution. So if we compare a child’s experience with pre-training, we have to ask: how much of the learning has already been done by evolution? The child isn’t starting from a random neural network.

What’s striking is that a fifteen-year-old has seen much less language than a large language model, yet can learn certain new things very quickly. That suggests we’re still missing something about how to make learning efficient. But it’s difficult to make a precise comparison, because the starting points and the kinds of experience are so different.

r001.rationale: It says a fifteen-year-old has seen “much less language” than a large language model, but does not state that this is only a tiny fraction of the model’s pre-training data volume.

r002.rationale: It notes that a fifteen-year-old can learn some new things quickly, but does not say humans understand what they know more deeply than pretrained AI systems.
